title: Kansuke Yamamoto (artist)
summary: Kansuke Yamamoto (山本 悍右, Yamamoto Kansuke; 30 March 1914 – 2 April 1987) was a Japanese avant-garde artist—active as a photographer and poet—whose practice, shaped by Surrealism, developed in dialogue with international modernism as it circulated into Japan in the 1930s and 1940s; amid intensifying ideological surveillance, Getty curator Amanda Maddox argues that Surrealism functioned for him not merely as an imported style but as an “attitude and a way of life,” through which he sustained imaginative freedom and nonconformity under constraint. In The International Encyclopedia of Surrealism, Yuko Ishii and Michael Richardson single him out as a particularly distinctive practitioner within twentieth-century Japanese photography, and historian Ryūichi Kaneko has described his 1932 collage The Developing Thought of a Human … Mist and Bedroom as a landmark in the formation of modern Japanese photography. Scholars and curators have framed Yamamoto’s work as a translation of Surrealist procedures rather than a belated imitation of European models, emphasizing his use of vernacular Japanese objects and his treatment of the photographic print as a constructed medium through techniques such as photomontage, photograms, and combination printing. Critic Kōtarō Iizawa has highlighted Yamamoto’s 1956 multi-image sequence My Thin-Aired Room (空気のうすいぼくの部屋)—now in the collection of the J. Paul Getty Museum—as an unusually early, constructed photographic “sequence” in Japan, noting that it was made more than a decade before Duane Michals began publishing his influential sequence works in the late 1960s. His work has been reassessed through major museum exhibitions—including Japan’s Modern Divide (Getty, 2013) and Surrealism Beyond Borders (the Metropolitan Museum of Art; Tate Modern, 2021–2022)—and is held in collections such as the J. Paul Getty Museum and the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA), which acquired his 1949 photograph Icarus’s Episode in 2025 (object number 310.2025).
full_text:
Kansuke Yamamoto (山本 悍右, Yamamoto Kansuke; 30 March 1914 – 2 April 1987) was a Japanese avant-garde artist—active as a photographer and poet—whose practice, shaped by Surrealism, developed in dialogue with international modernism as it circulated into Japan in the 1930s and 1940s; amid intensifying ideological surveillance, Getty curator Amanda Maddox argues that Surrealism functioned for him not merely as an imported style but as an “attitude and a way of life,” through which he sustained imaginative freedom and nonconformity under constraint. In The International Encyclopedia of Surrealism, Yuko Ishii and Michael Richardson single him out as a particularly distinctive practitioner within twentieth-century Japanese photography, and historian Ryūichi Kaneko has described his 1932 collage The Developing Thought of a Human … Mist and Bedroom as a landmark in the formation of modern Japanese photography. Scholars and curators have framed Yamamoto’s work as a translation of Surrealist procedures rather than a belated imitation of European models, emphasizing his use of vernacular Japanese objects and his treatment of the photographic print as a constructed medium through techniques such as photomontage, photograms, and combination printing. Critic Kōtarō Iizawa has highlighted Yamamoto’s 1956 multi-image sequence My Thin-Aired Room (空気のうすいぼくの部屋)—now in the collection of the J. Paul Getty Museum—as an unusually early, constructed photographic “sequence” in Japan, noting that it was made more than a decade before Duane Michals began publishing his influential sequence works in the late 1960s. His work has been reassessed through major museum exhibitions—including Japan’s Modern Divide (Getty, 2013) and Surrealism Beyond Borders (the Metropolitan Museum of Art; Tate Modern, 2021–2022)—and is held in collections such as the J. Paul Getty Museum and the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA), which acquired his 1949 photograph Icarus’s Episode in 2025 (object number 310.2025).

Early life and background (1914–1930)
Birth and early life
Yamamoto was born Kansuke Yamamoto on 30 March 1914 in Teppōmachi, Naka-ku, Nagoya, Aichi Prefecture. His father, Gorō Yamamoto, ran Yamamoto Goro Shoten, an early photographic-equipment business in the city, and was active in local amateur-photography circles during the Taishō period. Contemporary accounts of Nagoya’s art-photography scene place Gorō within circles including the Aiyū Photo Club (Aiyū Shashin Kurabu), planned in 1911 and formally established in January 1912, whose monthly meetings were sometimes held at the family camera shop. Growing up inside a family trade that linked cameras, materials, and club culture gave Yamamoto an unusually concrete understanding of photography’s infrastructures—knowledge that later surfaced in his insistence on print quality, publishing design, and the social life of images. More broadly, the annual Kenten competitions organized by the Tokyo Photographic Research Society attracted submissions from across Japan, including Nagoya, linking local club cultures to a national exhibition circuit.

Photographic milieu and early technical fluency
Nagoya’s photographic culture in the early twentieth century was shaped by amateur “art photography” circles; the Aiyū Shashin Club (planned in 1911; formally established in January 1912) became known for pigment printing practices such as gum bichromate (“Aiyū no gomu”), and for an exhibition-and-salon model that helped sustain local photographic production. Sources on Yamamoto’s early environment describe his father, Gorō, as a pivotal figure in this community: he co-founded the Aiyū Photography Club (Aiyū Shashin Club), described as the region's largest amateur organization, and served as its representative during the Taishō period. A Nagoya City Art Museum publication further records that the club’s secretariat was located at Yamamoto Goro Shoten on Hirokoji-dori in Sakae, central Nagoya, positioning the family business at the operational center of the city’s photographic network. Gorō’s photo studio and camera shop also created an environment that familiarized Yamamoto early with photographic materials and processes. A chronology compiled by Yamamoto Toshio records that Yamamoto later, around 1936, helped establish the A.B.C.P.C. (ABC Photo Club) within Yamamoto Goro Shoten. This sustained proximity to materials, cameras, and darkroom culture shaped Yamamoto’s technical fluency from an unusually young age.

Nagoya’s photographic ecology and artist-run print culture
Accounts of Yamamoto’s formation situate him within a city whose photographic culture has been characterized by a dense ecology of studios, camera shops, clubs, and artist-run publications. Read biographically, this ecology clarifies what it meant for Yamamoto to come of age in Nagoya: photography was not only an aesthetic pursuit but also a visible urban infrastructure of studios, dealers, processing services, and club activity that could sustain production and circulation. Takeba quantifies this ecology in concrete terms: Ōsu alone supported numerous commercial studios in the early twentieth century, and by May 1925 the city counted dozens of operating portrait studios; the number of photo-material dealers likewise expanded rapidly by the mid-1930s. In a museum newsletter, the Nagoya City Art Museum notes that Nagoya was once regarded as one of Japan’s foremost “holy lands” of photography, tracing a local lineage of photographic expression back to the Aiyū Photography Club—co-founded by Yamamoto’s father, Gorō—planned in 1911 and formally established in January 1912. The idea of Nagoya as a “photographic city” was articulated as early as 1911, when pictorialist photographer Chōtarō Hidaka argued for building a strong local club culture that could advance photographic art collectively in the city.
For Yamamoto’s later practice, the significance of this background lies not only in abundance of photographic activity but in the local standards and techniques through which photographs were made and judged. Curator Jō Takeba further notes that Nagoya’s early twentieth-century “art photography” milieu coalesced around the Aiyū Photography Club and was shaped by pictorialist print practices in which finishing processes—such as gum-bichromate printing and retouch—were treated as integral to expression. Surveying the longer arc of Nagoya’s modern photography, Takeba argues that the city’s movements twice exerted national influence: first through the early-1920s pictorialist moment centered on the Aiyū Photography Club under Chōtarō Hidaka, and later through the late-1930s emergence of “avant-garde photography” as Nagoya photographers engaged abstraction and Surrealism as competing—and sometimes coordinated—programs. He also stresses that Aiyū’s earlier dominance functioned as a local orthodoxy that could produce stagnation, making the region’s later embrace of “New Photography” distinctive in its explicitly “de-Aiyū” self-understanding—an effort to break the pictorialist hold while redefining the city’s photographic identity on new terms. In this account, the early-1930s push toward a post-pictorialist “New Photography” idiom was led less by Tokyo or Nagoya than by Kansai circles, whose exhibitions and magazine-mediated visibility helped consolidate a new horizon of “avant-garde photography” across Japan. He further records that by 1921 Aiyū photographers had gained national visibility in major competitive exhibitions, and that the early 1920s saw a turn among younger practitioners toward bromide prints emphasizing light, tonal contrast, and compositional rhythm.
This same infrastructure—shops, services, and periodicals—also helps explain how Yamamoto’s generation could encounter new technical and aesthetic vocabularies as part of everyday photographic life rather than solely through elite institutions. Takeba links Nagoya’s “photographic city” identity in the 1930s to the rapid expansion of amateur practice and to the emergence of specialist photo-processing and printing businesses that mediated between clubs and hobbyists. He points to Narita Haruyō’s “photo-technology shop” on Hirokōji / Sakae-kōji as an early hub that gathered numerous amateurs and helped normalize darkroom practice as an everyday service. By the mid-1930s, this infrastructure could sustain Nagoya-based periodicals: Takeba records that the monthly magazine Cameraman (launched in October 1936) sold out its first print run of 5,000 copies, suggesting the scale of the local photographic public. Takeba further records that wartime constraints soon bore directly on this magazine culture: in October 1940, after the proofs for Cameraman No.50 were completed, editor-in-chief Jiro Nagata was summoned by the prefectural police Special Higher Police and was compelled to terminate the magazine on the grounds that, under the “high national defense state,” it should be discontinued in accordance with resource policy—an episode that makes visible how quickly the infrastructural conditions of photographic modernism could be curtailed.
The same account emphasizes that the city sustained itself as a “photographic city” across successive periods not only through individual works but also through the publication of journals, bulletins, and photobooks that circulated programs and aesthetic positions beyond the region. For a biography of Yamamoto, these publishing circuits matter because they form the practical preconditions for the later roles he assumed as a maker and mediator of photographic and literary avant-gardes.
Museum narratives of the period emphasize that, by the late 1930s, avant-garde photography associated with Nagoya attracted nationwide attention, and that postwar Surrealist and experimental tendencies in the region remained in active tension with realist currents that dominated broader critical accounts. Within this context, Yamamoto’s later roles as an editor, publisher, and organizer can be understood not as ancillary to his practice but as structural to how avant-garde photography was sustained and transmitted. An exhibition text published by MEM likewise frames 1930s experimental photography in Japan as a nationwide phenomenon sustained by amateur clubs in regional cities, and situates Nagoya’s collectives—including Nagoya Photo Gruppe (1934) and Nagoya Photo Avant-Garde (1939)—as key nodes in this milieu.
Against this backdrop, Yamamoto’s early-1930s shift toward constructed and experimental approaches can be read as emerging from, and reacting to, the city’s established club culture, technical standards, and publication networks.  In the early 1930s, he began to translate these local infrastructures into a distinctive avant-garde practice as new photographic and literary vocabularies circulated through Japan.

Prewar avant-garde practice (1931–1937)
Encounter with Surrealism and the French transmission
Francophone channels and Surrealism’s literary transmission
Yamamoto’s first sustained encounter with Surrealism took shape through channels that were at once explicitly Francophone and broadly European in their intellectual reach. Aoki notes that Chirū (Tiroux) Yamanaka—an advocate for Surrealism in Japan—corresponded with Paul Éluard and André Breton and translated Surrealist writings, forming part of the cultural circuitry through which French Surrealist ideas entered Japan’s literary and artistic spheres; one such conduit was Yamanaka’s poetry magazine cine´. Munro likewise notes that Yamamoto first encountered Surrealism through reading Yamanaka’s journal CINÉ, and that he later collaborated with Yamanaka when the title re-emerged as Yoru no Funsui from 1938. Tani adds that Yamamoto’s discovery of Surrealism was mediated by literary magazines, citing titles such as Shi to shiron and CINÉ (published by Chirū (Tiroux) Yamanaka). Iizawa notes that Yamamoto began writing poems around 1930, at the age of sixteen, and that through the Surrealist poetry circle surrounding cინე´ he established early connections with figures such as Shūzō Takiguchi and Chirū (Tiroux) Yamanaka, both often credited with fostering Surrealism in Japan. A chronology compiled by Yamamoto Toshio records that between 1930 and 1932 he wrote 44 poems in a cycle titled The Revelation of Nonsense (Japanese: 南仙子黙示録), with a final poem added in 1936.

Tokyo study, return to Nagoya, and Surrealism as method
According to the Getty Museum, Yamamoto left Nagoya around 1929 to study French poetry and literature in Tokyo and, upon returning, began writing poems and producing collages before turning to photography as a Surrealist instrument. He had already begun writing poetry as a teenager—around the age of fifteen—and that literary practice remained inseparable from his visual work; in the same formative period, he encountered Surrealism and Dada through small magazines and through the activities of Nagoya-based poets and critics introducing these movements in Japan. 
Kaneko notes that after graduating from the Nagoya City Commercial School in 1929, Yamamoto also studied French at the Athénée Français language school in Tokyo before entering Meiji University to read French literature and poetry. During this period in Tokyo, he encountered Western avant-garde movements and theories—including Surrealism, Dada, and related developments in modernist art and design—before leaving the university after a short period; he returned to Nagoya in 1931 and committed himself to developing a Surrealist vocabulary within both photography and poetry.
In a chronology compiled by Yamamoto Toshio, Yamamoto is recorded as beginning poetry in 1930; through modernist and Surrealist-oriented poetry journals—including Nagoya-based publications—he encountered figures such as Chirū Yamanaka and other writers who were translating, circulating, and debating European avant-gardes. In a later interview, he recalled that he turned seriously to photography in the early 1930s because Surrealism had already entered Japan and “it might be possible to do it with photography as well,” treating the medium not as reportage but as a method for constructing thought through images. Masachika Tani, a professor at Waseda University, argues that Yamamoto turned to photography in the early 1930s as an extension of his avant-garde poetry, pursuing Surrealism as a visual method rather than a separate, purely photographic interest.

Formation of an avant-garde practice (1931–1937)
“New Photography” and publication-centered experimentation
Photography critic Kōtarō Iizawa situates Yamamoto’s emergence within a broader turning point in Japanese photographic expression in the 1930s, when pictorialist “Art Photography” (Geijutsu Shashin) increasingly gave way to Shinkō Shashin (New Photography) as photographers sought methods capable of responding to rapidly transforming urban environments in the wake of the 1923 Great Kantō earthquake. He identifies the 1931 German International Traveling Photography Exhibition in Tokyo and Osaka (a selection from Stuttgart’s 1929 Film und Foto) as a key catalyst, introducing Japanese photographers to photograms, photomontage, small-camera snapshots of cityscapes, X-ray images, and microscopic photography—experimental approaches that accelerated the turn toward New Photography. Within this milieu, Yamamoto positioned himself as a practitioner of New Photography, treating photographic modernism not merely as a repertoire of stylistic effects but as an intellectual method—one capable of reordering perception and, by extension, the social imagination.
In early theoretical statements of the movement, writers such as Nobuo Ina and Shigemine Kanamaru emphasized objective depiction and the discovery of new beauty, photography as a record and report of lived reality, and form constructed through light—criteria that distinguished “New Photography” from pictorialist “art photography.”

Dokuritsu and early participation in collective print networks
From the outset, Yamamoto entered photography through print-based collectives rather than through salons alone. In October 1931 he became a founding member of the Dokuritsu Shashin Kenkyūkai (Independent Photography Research Group), which launched the journal Dokuritsu the following month. Across early issues he contributed photographs alongside short theoretical texts on titles and themes, and in 1932 published a collage work later preserved in the Nagoya City Art Museum—evidence that montage and the constructed print were central to his practice well before his better-known Surrealist sequences of the late 1930s and 1940s.
In 1931, at the age of seventeen, Yamamoto joined the Dokuritsu Shashin Kenkyū Kai (Independent Photography Research Association), which a Nagoya City Art Museum account notes was founded at his father’s shop, Yamamoto Goro Shoten in Sakae. In the same year, he began publishing his work in the journal Dokuritsu (Independent), issued by the Dokuritsu Shashin Kenkyū Kai, an early platform that signaled both his commitment to the avant-garde and his readiness to participate in collective, publication-centered forms of practice that would remain crucial throughout his career. In an English-language survey of the period, Takeba describes Yamamoto as a young Nagoya poet who began photographing in 1931 and, the following year, published critically acclaimed photo-collages in a small-press magazine while remaining active as a Surrealist photographer through the 1930s. According to Takeba, the Dokuritsu Shashin Kenkyū Kai was established in Nagoya in October 1931 by Shimizu Kentarō (志水賢太郎), Tomita Hachirō (富多八郎), and Okonogi Mitsuya (小此木光也). It began with sixteen members and its bulletin Dokuritsu is currently confirmed in four issues through B.2 (April 1932). Takeba further situates Dokuritsu in the interval between Tokyo’s journal Shinkō Shashin Kenkyū ending (July 1931) and the launch of the monthly magazine Kōga (May 1932), framing the Nagoya bulletin as a transitional node where the terms of 1930s photographic experimentation were tested and argued in print. Fujimura notes that the Shinkō Shashin Kenkyūkai—often treated as Tokyo-centred—also included participants linked to Kansai’s Naniwa Shashin Club and Nagoya’s Dokuritsu Shashin Kenkyūkai. 
A Nagoya City Art Museum account further notes that he produced highly accomplished, sharply critical photo-collages during this period, though his talent was not yet widely known beyond this local circle.
In the B.1 issue, Yamamoto also published an essay titled Dai to shudai (“Title and Subject”), arguing that photographic work should articulate the content of an “ism” and the artist’s conscious intention rather than allow a title to become an absolute substitute for meaning. Takeba reproduces Yamamoto’s formulation: “It is necessary to express the theme of our ideology and the content of our consciousness.” Takeba reads this early critique—written when Yamamoto was still seventeen—as a warning against the tendency of “New Photography” to lean on opaque, affective titles once the movement began circulating more widely through periodicals.

Kaneko records that reproductions from Yamamoto’s early photocollage series The Developing Thought of a Human… circulated through Dokuritsu, appearing in the journal’s B1 issue (1 January 1932) and B2 issue (5 April 1932). He notes that the two works reproduced in B1 are no longer extant, but suggests that they were also photocollages—evidence that Yamamoto’s Surrealist experiments were publicly legible in print from the outset. Such publication-based activity was especially consequential in Nagoya, where journals and bulletins functioned as both exhibition spaces and intellectual infrastructure for the avant-garde. A chronology compiled by Yamamoto Toshio records that he joined the Nihon Genteiban Club (Mikasa Shobō) in February 1933, and in February 1934 also joined the Shunchōkai Genteiban Kurabu and the Book Club. Yamamoto’s early visibility in print thus prefigured the editorial and organizing work through which he would later help consolidate the city’s experimental circles. Discussing the same early phase, Iizawa describes Yamamoto’s photocollage The Developing Thought of a Human... Mist and Bedroom (1932)—published in Dokuritsu—as a collage that juxtaposes an image of lips with fragments cut from contemporary newspapers, and argues that this work indicates Yamamoto had already acquired an avant-garde photographic idiom by the age of eighteen. Tani notes that the collage incorporates newspaper fragments referring to the 1932 Geneva disarmament conference and to the economic crisis following the 1929 New York stock-market crash, juxtaposed with cut-out sensual imagery.

Prewar activity and a Paris-oriented Surrealist horizon
Surrealism in Japan and a Paris-facing horizon
Maddox situates the Japanese reception of Surrealism in the interwar decades—from the aftermath of the Great Kantō Earthquake (1923) to the onset of World War II—when debates over modernity and political expression sharpened the movement’s stakes in Japan. She notes that Japan was among the earliest countries outside Europe to register Surrealism’s impact, yet the movement’s reception in Japan has been uneven, as Surrealist art has not always been integrated into canonical histories of Japanese art. Surrealist ideas circulated in Japan early: Misao Harada notes that surrealist poems were already being disseminated by 1925, that new groups formed from 1927, and that by 1929 the first Japanese paintings explicitly claiming the “surrealist” label had appeared. In the catalogue foreword for Surrealism Beyond Borders, the editors note that in 1935 the Surrealist poet Benjamin Péret argued for Surrealism’s international character and listed Japan among the places where it was already present, underscoring the movement’s early global diffusion.
Taka Ishii Gallery describes Yamamoto as one of the leading figures of Surrealist photography in Japan, highlighting his sharp eye for social criticism and a distinctive poetic sensibility.
Yamamoto’s early practice developed at the moment when Japanese “New Photography” and avant-garde photography were oriented toward experimentation and new modes of expression; the Getty characterizes Surrealism as “the backbone of progressive photography in Japan in the 1930s,” and places Yamamoto among the innovative artists who advanced this movement by merging European-inspired Surrealist iconography with distinctly Japanese motifs and concerns. Art criticism has also described Nagoya as one of the centres of Surrealism in Japan, a context in which Yamamoto’s prewar activity gains particular specificity as both local practice and part of a broader, transregional avant-garde. In a study of Surrealism’s regional reception, Hanako Takayama (Meiji University) frames Nagoya as a node of multidirectional circulation rather than a one-way diffusion from Tokyo. The catalogue introduction to Surrealism Beyond Borders similarly treats Japan’s interwar photographic circles as part of Surrealism’s wider geography, explicitly placing the amateur photo clubs founded in Nagoya and Osaka alongside the Parisian Bureau de recherches surréalistes as comparable sites of collective activity and exchange. Art historian Majella Munro challenges the “core–periphery” framing that casts Japanese Surrealism as a late-developing, poorly informed echo of Paris, arguing that it rests on an overstated assumption of isolation. She notes that leading Japanese practitioners were active in Paris and that sustained correspondence linked Japanese writers and artists to European Surrealists from the 1920s and 1930s, making international exchange integral to the movement’s development in Japan.

1937 exhibition and the international legitimation of Surrealism in Japan
Munro highlights an earlier milestone: the 1932 Paris–Tokio League of Rising Art exhibition—curated by André Breton and presenting work by several European Surrealists—as evidence that Surrealist work was exhibited in Japan prior to the 1937 exhibition often treated as a turning point.
Harada further reports that epistolary exchanges between Shūzō Takiguchi and André Breton (from around 1930) and between Tiroux Yamanaka and Paul Éluard (from 1933) led to concrete collaborative projects, including the Tokyo-edited publication L'Échange surréaliste (1936) and the Exposition surréaliste of 1937 staged in several major Japanese cities. Both Takiguchi and Yamanaka were also listed in the Dictionnaire abrégé du surréalisme (1938), a catalogue associated with the Paris Exposition internationale du surréalisme.
Within this climate, an explicitly international milestone shaped the Japanese Surrealist scene: Aoki notes that the poet–critic Shūzō Takiguchi organized a seminal Surrealist exhibition in Japan in 1937 with the support of European Surrealists, including André Breton and Paul Éluard—an event that clarified both the intellectual stakes and the international legitimacy of Surrealism in Japan.
Munro further notes that in a manuscript on “Surrealism and Photography” dated 1940, Yamamoto complained of increasing totalitarianism in Japan and reflected on the difficulty of aligning Surrealism with Communism. Quoting Breton’s Communicating Vessels, he questioned how Surrealism’s notion of compulsive beauty could be made to serve Communist aims, concluding that the movement’s inherent liberalism ultimately undermined any stable rapprochement—while still insisting on the revolutionary potential of his photographic practice.
Munro adds that Yamamoto expressed an interest in Communism in diary entries from 1933–1934, underscoring that his engagement with left politics was not merely retrospective but part of his prewar intellectual horizon.
Taken together, Munro presents these diary and manuscript materials as evidence that Yamamoto was engaging—while based in Japan—with Surrealism’s wider debates over whether revolutionary politics could be reconciled with Surrealist aesthetics and its notion of compulsive beauty.

Editorial Surrealism: Yoru no Funsui and Francophone signals
Francophone circuits: correspondence and translation
Taken together, these circumstances place Yamamoto’s Surrealism within a historically specific, Paris-facing field of transmission rather than a belated provincial echo. Aoki’s account of Takiguchi’s 1937 exhibition—organized with support from European Surrealists including André Breton and Paul Éluard—alongside Yamanaka Chirū’s correspondence with Breton and Éluard and his translations of Surrealist writings, indicates that Japanese Surrealism developed in active relation to Francophone interlocutors and texts. Munro also points to the 1932 “Paris–Tokyo League of Emerging Artists” exhibition (curated by Breton) as evidence that Surrealist works were being exhibited in Japan prior to the better-known 1937 overseas Surrealism exhibition circuit. Maddox notes that Yamamoto built a substantial personal library of Surrealist writings in French (including volumes by Breton, Éluard, Aragon, Péret, and Soupault) and read Freud, indicating that his engagement was grounded in literature and theory as well as visual models. Munro further records that Yamamoto was fluent in French and maintained an extensive Surrealist library, subscribing to the periodicals Acéphale and Cahiers d’Art alongside French-language Surrealist books and journals circulating in Japan. In 1936, a chronology compiled by Yamamoto Toshio records that he began ordering overseas publications, including the periodical Cahiers d’Art and books published by G.L.M. Munro also notes Yamanaka’s attraction to “dissident” Surrealisms associated with Georges Bataille, a context that helps situate the Nagoya circle’s orientation within intra-Surrealist debates rather than a single orthodox line of transmission.
Yamamoto’s subsequent turn toward editing and publishing—above all his founding of ''Yoru no Funsui''—can therefore
be read as a contemporaneous effort to translate Surrealist procedure into a Japanese visual–poetic idiom at the very moment when the movement’s international legitimacy was being asserted in Japan. Munro notes that Freudian ideas circulated in Japan from around 1926 and gained a measure of popularity in the 1930s, often being interpreted in relation to local ethical and religious frameworks—conditions that shaped how Surrealists in Japan approached the unconscious and complicate accounts that treat Japanese Surrealist engagements with psychoanalysis as merely second-hand or superficial. In Munro’s account, the Nagoya milieu in which Yamamoto and Yamanaka worked shows a marked interest in dissident strands of Surrealism, contrasted with the more orthodox, Breton-centered line associated with Shūzō Takiguchi in Tokyo.

Editorial platforms: Yoru no Funsui and Carnet Bleu
Taka Ishii Gallery reports that Yamamoto was inspired by this 1937 exhibition to found the Surrealist poetry journal Yoru no Funsui (The Night’s Fountain). The journal functioned as a forum for Surrealist ideas in which Yamamoto published poems, texts, drawings, and photographs; according to the Getty, he ceased publishing when the Tokkō (a special police force) expressed concern about its contents, underscoring the proximity of his Surrealism to the realities of wartime surveillance and censorship. Oxford Brookes University art historian Jelena Stojković further reports that Yoru no funsui (1938–1939) was banned by the police, and that Yamamoto was interrogated on the political implications of Surrealist photography—an episode that clarifies the coercive wartime pressures under which his editorial Surrealism persisted. In “The World in the Time of the Surrealists,” D'Alessandro and Gale frame such periodicals as not secondary to major artworks but as a primary material infrastructure for Surrealism’s transmission, enabling exchange, translation, and relay between communities even when texts and images could not be immediately or uniformly absorbed across languages and locations.

Seidōsha and Carnet Bleu: a French title in late-1930s Nagoya
In 1938, in parallel with his editorial work, Yamamoto also helped establish the photographers’ group Seidōsha (Blue Admiration Society) and began publishing a newsletter titled Carnet Bleu(surviving issues 1941–1942)—a deliberate French title that signaled his sustained identification with the Francophone avant-garde even as cultural nationalism intensified in late-1930s Japan. A 1989 Nagoya City Art Museum exhibition catalogue notes that around 1938 Yamamoto became acquainted with photographer Keiichiro Goto through the Seidōsha circle, and that the two remained close thereafter.
Kaneko further reports that the fifth and final issue (10 August 1942) printed Yamamoto’s Japanese translation of Philippe Soupault’s essay État de la photographie (“The Present State of Photography”), underscoring his sustained engagement with Francophone Surrealist writing during the war years. Takeba adds that Yamamoto appended a brief note to the translation that measures Soupault’s anti-fascist formulation against the wartime discourse of “national mission” circulating in Nagoya’s avant-garde circles, registering the pressure to align photographic practice with state-sanctioned objectives.

Nagoya networks and photomontage in “New Photography”
From the early 1930s Yamamoto emerged as a central figure in Nagoya’s avant-garde circles, producing photographs and photomontages attentive to international Surrealism while grounded in the textures of Japanese daily life. He became involved with local groups and publications associated with the “New Photography” (Shinkō Shashin) movement, helping shape a modernist photographic culture in Nagoya through collaboration, editing, and exhibiting.
In Japanese usage, the term Shinkō Shashin (“New Photography”) emerged around 1930, and later scholarship notes that networks beyond Tokyo—including photographers connected to Kansai circles and Nagoya’s Independent Photography Research Association—were involved in its early formation.
A key early work, the hand-colored collage photograph Aru Ningen no Shisou no Hatten・・・Moya to Shinshitsu(The Developing Thought of a Human: Mist and Bedroom) (1932), is often cited as among his earliest extant statements in photomontage and is held by the Nagoya City Art Museum—an institutional anchor for his local significance even as later reception became international. Photography historian Ryūichi Kaneko reports that the date of Yamamoto’s photocollage The Developing Thought of a Human … Mist and Bedroom(Nagoya City Art Museum)—long uncertain—was established as 1932 during research for the 2001 retrospective Surrealist Yamamoto Kansuke, and argues that this redating repositions the work as a landmark for understanding the formation of modern Japanese photography in the 1930s.
Kaneko describes The Developing Thought of a Human … Mist and Bedroom (created when the artist was only eighteen) as a hand-colored photocollage whose surface is physically torn open to expose inserted newspaper clippings, over which Yamamoto arranges disembodied fragments—most notably repeated lips, a woman’s high-heeled leg, and a small portrait head—so that Surrealist disjunction is staged as a materially constructed operation on the print rather than a seamless photographic illusion; the visible headlines themselves turn on arms reduction and abrupt movements in the yen.
Stojković notes that Yamamoto was already working through photomontage and collage procedures in the early 1930s within Surrealist circles in Nagoya, and argues that these printed experiments—embedded in a wider Surrealist “constellation” of exchange and collaboration among poets, critics, and photographers—amounted to an “impossible avant-garde,” produced under conditions that rendered experimental art politically precarious and materially difficult to sustain.
Discussing the work as it appeared in Dokuritsu, Takeba emphasizes that its montage of bodily fragments, revue imagery, urban elements, and contemporary newspaper reports (including coverage of disarmament negotiations) does not remain at the level of fragmentary modernism but prompts the viewer to infer time and narrative—an early sign of Yamamoto’s explicitly critical direction.
From the outset, Yamamoto’s Surrealism developed as a practice of translation rather than imitation: international avant-garde devices—collage, discontinuous spatial logic, and the “found” object—were re-situated in recognizably Japanese settings and materials. This approach would later become central to curatorial arguments that place him among the most conceptually ambitious Japanese photographers of the prewar and early postwar period.

Language as medium: the 1936 name change
In 1936 Yamamoto altered the written characters of his given name from 勘助 to 悍右 (still read “Kansuke”). In a later account, art historian John Solt—drawing on testimony from the photographer Katsuhiko Okazaki—interpreted the change as a deliberately charged, activist gesture aimed at the “violent right,” indicating the degree to which Yamamoto understood language itself as a political medium rather than a neutral label.
A chronology compiled by Yamamoto Toshio records that in 1936 Yamamoto held his first solo exhibition at Maruzen Gallery in Nagoya.
In the wake of the 1937 ''Kaigai Chōgenjitsushugi Sakuhinten'' (''Exhibition of Overseas Surrealist Works''), Yamamoto’s ambitions as an editor and publisher sharpened markedly. An exhibition catalogue notes that he attended the Nagoya presentation repeatedly and came to see the need for a periodical to convey Surrealist ideas. Yamamoto later recalled discussing with Chirū Yamanaka the need to promote Surrealism through publishing; the initiative became a catalyst for launching the Surrealist periodical ''Yoru no funsui'' (1938–1939).

International context: contemporaneity and translation rather than imitation
While Surrealism in Japan was historically criticized as an "imported" movement and dismissed as mere imitation, recent scholarship has complicated this reception. Literary scholar Satoru Hashimoto has proposed approaching the Japanese reception of Surrealism through “transculturation,” emphasizing the complex forms of reworking undertaken in the receiving context rather than a one-way transfer from Paris.
As early as 1930, Japanese critic Takenaka Kyūshichi warned against a purely Breton-centered, fashion-driven reception of Surrealism—evidence that debates over orthodoxy and autonomy accompanied the movement’s Japanese uptake from the outset.
In Munro’s account, Japanese Surrealists actively sought “indigenous antecedents” rather than treating Surrealism as a fixed European style to be copied, drawing in particular on Zen-inflected cultural forms and practices as resources for avant-garde experimentation. She cautions that claims that Japanese Surrealists were merely “playing at being European” are amplified when domestic precedents are ignored; instead, she proposes a model in which Surrealist procedures in Japan assimilated local referents while generating new, culturally specific forms of critique.
These prewar episodes locate Yamamoto not as a provincial follower but as a contemporaneous participant in a transnational Surrealist moment. The 1937 exhibition’s documented support from Breton and Éluard, together with the correspondence and translation networks described by Aoki, demonstrate that Japanese Surrealism developed in active relation to Paris rather than in isolation. Within that historically specific horizon, Yamamoto’s turn to “practicing Surrealism in photography” (as later summarized in artist chronologies) can be read as an effort to translate Surrealist procedure—collage logic, disjunctive space, and emblematic objects—into a distinctly Japanese visual-poetic language, a synthesis the Getty describes as both innovative and central to Japan’s avant-garde photographic movement.
Art historian John Solt argues that Yamamoto's engagement with European Surrealism is best understood as a form of translation and dialogue rather than simple imitation, suggesting that particular works can be read in conversation with figures such as Salvador Dalí, Joan Miró, Man Ray, René Magritte, and Jean Arp. Solt further contrasts Yamamoto's compositional restraint—especially his willingness to leave space blank—with the more visually saturated imagery often associated with Western Surrealist photography, presenting understatement and subtlety as distinctive features of his approach.
Maddox develops this “translation rather than imitation” model at the level of compositional structure, noting that Yamamoto repeatedly engaged canonical Surrealist images as templates to be re-staged and re-authored. She reports, for example, that Yamamoto sketched Magritte’s Man with a Newspaper (1928) from Julien Levy’s 1936 volume Surrealism—including Levy’s alternate title, “Now You Don’t”—and that the work later served as a model for Yamamoto’s four-part photographic suite My Thin-Aired Room (1956), which turns a single pictorial conceit of disappearance into a sequential narrative.

Publishing and wartime constraints (1938–1945)
Art criticism has also described Nagoya as one of the centres of Surrealism in Japan, a context in which Yamamoto and his peers sustained avant-garde photographic activity across the prewar and postwar decades.

Publishing as avant-garde infrastructure
From 1938, Yamamoto’s work and influence expanded through editing and publishing—roles that were crucial in Japanese avant-garde culture, where journals functioned as both exhibition spaces and ideological platforms. An estate chronology records that between 1933 and 1935 Yamamoto joined the Mingei magazine Kōgei and participated in several limited-edition and bibliophile circles, including the Nihon Genteiban Club, the Shōchōkai Limited Edition Club, the Shomotsu Club, Mazu, and the Nihon Aishokai. The catalogue Surrealism Beyond Borders emphasizes that periodicals—alongside radio and film—were among the primary infrastructures through which Surrealism circulated internationally: Surrealist groups often defined their affinities through journals that disseminated poetry, polemics, translations, reproductions, and exhibition news, and in some contexts operated in tandem with local exhibitions. Cole likewise notes that questionnaires published in such journals enabled dispersed participants to read and respond to one another’s ideas, producing a multi-voiced, composite portrait of Surrealism rather than the singular voice of a manifesto. Munro further cites Takiguchi’s diary remark that Surrealism’s development in Japan was “completed” through the art world’s interest in it, underscoring the institutional conditions through which the movement was disseminated and historicized. More broadly, D’Alessandro and Gale argue that Surrealism repeatedly cohered through portable, collective formats and sites of encounter—an emphasis that aligns Yamamoto’s commitment to small-scale publishing and group-based activity with the movement’s international modes of relay.
Survey scholarship has also reframed Surrealism’s early Parisian infrastructure as networked communication rather than a one-way “export” model. In Surrealism Beyond Borders, Sean O’Hanlan revisits the Bureau de recherches surréalistes (Paris, 1924–25) as an organe de liaison whose public-facing work—logbooks, visitors, and the circulation of leaflets and La révolution surréaliste through subscriptions and press correspondence—helps demonstrate that Surrealism functioned as a shifting transnational assemblage from its origins. In this framework, Yamamoto’s own editorial and publishing activity can likewise be approached as part of Surrealism’s material infrastructure in Japan: periodicals and small publications not as secondary ephemera, but as primary relay mechanisms through which procedures, images, and vocabularies were exchanged under conditions of surveillance and censorship. 
In Nagoya, where such platforms were unusually central to artistic life, the act of editing and publishing carried heightened stakes: it shaped both the circulation of Surrealist ideas and the visibility of their practitioners. The suppression of Yamamoto’s editorial projects under Tokkō scrutiny therefore registers not only as an episode of censorship but as a disruption of the city’s avant-garde infrastructure. A comparative case discussed in the same catalogue is De Schone Zakdoek (The Clean Kerchief), a hand-made single-copy journal produced clandestinely in Utrecht between 1941 and 1944; its domestic, private circulation illustrates how Surrealist periodicals could function as both underground publication and serial work of art under wartime censorship.

Tokkō scrutiny and the material conditions of dissent
He organized the Nagoya-based group Seidōsha (青憧社) and edited its bulletin Carnet Bleu, notable for retaining a French title through a period of intensifying cultural nationalism.
A decisive turn came with Yamamoto’s work as an editor–publisher. In November 1938 he launched the Surrealist poetry and art journal Yoru no Funsui (The Night’s Fountain)—which, according to a City of Nagoya profile, he edited with Shōko Ema, Katsue Kitasono, Shirō Murano, and Chirū Yamanaka among others—issuing four numbers through October 1939 in small editions. Writing on Tiroux (Chirū) Yamanaka, Kurosawa notes that Yamanaka participated unreservedly in the project, and he describes the phrase “the night’s fountain” as evoking a mysterious, fantastic image that could, in the context of Japan moving toward war, figure an emblem of enduring poetry emerging from darkness. Yamamoto did not treat the magazine as a mere container for texts: he pursued paper, typography, and layout as integral to meaning, solicited a heterogeneous circle of contributors across poetry, drawing, and photography, and used translation as a way to place Nagoya-based Surrealism in active relation to Francophone writing. The journal also included contributions by the VOU poet Katsue Kitasono. Cole stresses that cross-cultural transmission in Surrealist periodicals depended on intermediaries and strategically deployed translation, through which Surrealism could be refracted and resituated for different audiences and local political-aesthetic concerns. Bibliophile accounts later singled out Yoru no Funsui for its exceptional material standards—handmade papers and artisanal printing—presenting the journal itself as a Surrealist object as much as a literary forum.
In a profile by Shinzō Kinoshita, the journal is situated against the rapid intensification of militarism in the late 1930s—amid tightening speech controls and acute paper shortages in the wake of the February 26 Incident, the Marco Polo Bridge Incident, and the promulgation of the National Mobilization Law—a climate in which literary activity in Nagoya was described as having fallen into a marked lull. Distinct from the utilitarian print culture of the wartime period, Kinoshita describes the journal as emphasizing materiality through its use of high-quality handmade Izumo washi by the papermaker Eishirō Abe, later designated a holder of an Important Intangible Cultural Property (often glossed in English as a “Living National Treasure”) for gampi papermaking. Maddox adds that ''Yoru no Funsui'' deliberately fused literary translation with visual reproduction on this distinctively Japanese material: alongside translations of French Surrealist poetry and Yamamoto’s own poems, it included reproduced drawings by Yves Tanguy (originally made for Benjamin Péret’s ''Dormir, dormir dans les pierres''). An exhibition catalogue notes that Yoru no Funsui reproduced a portrait of Lautréamont drawn by Salvador Dalí and carried contributions by figures such as Kitasono Katsue and Yoshio Shimozato. She further notes that, physically transported by the poet Chirū (Tiroux) Yamanaka, copies of the journal were delivered directly into the hands of Paul Éluard in France. This confirms that Yamamoto’s practice established a tangible, material link with the Parisian avant-garde, operating as a two-way dialogue rather than a passive reception of Western influence.
This artistic autonomy, however, faced immediate suppression. Multiple accounts describe ''The Night’s Fountain'' as coming under pressure from Japan’s Special Higher Police (Tokkō) amid widening wartime surveillance and censorship under the Peace Preservation Law. Kinoshita records Yamamoto’s recollection that police intervention forced the cessation of the journal while the fifth issue was being printed, as its avant-garde content was deemed detrimental to public morale; the issue was never released and publication ceased after the fourth number. According to a chronology compiled by Yamamoto Toshio, after Yoru no Funsui ceased publication Yamamoto planned a Surrealism-focused journal titled Brille (Buriru), but the project remained unpublished.
Munro writes that Yamamoto’s Nagoya-based journal Yoru no Funsui was closed by police in 1939, and notes that during the investigation he was asked by the authorities how his “surreal photography” contributed to Japan’s war effort—an exchange that framed his practice as unacceptably radical rather than culturally useful to the state.
Munro also notes—citing Kaneko Ryūichi—that state demands for propagandistic output most directly constrained documentary photographers and photojournalists, even as avant-garde practice could still be scrutinized as ideologically suspect.
Tani also reports that during the 1939 investigation Yamamoto was pressed to explain lines from his poems. 
Regarding this intervention, Maddox cites an episode recorded by John Solt concerning a specific interrogation in 1940, in which the Thought Police questioned Yamamoto closely, demanding an explanation of "the third line of the second stanza" of a surrealist poem. Yamamoto adopted a strategy of intellectual resistance, recalling later that he aimed to "evade their questions while not saying anything that the police might interpret as incriminating," thereby outmaneuvering the interrogation through intellectual agility rather than open confrontation. Solt reports that Yamamoto was released only after agreeing not to publish further issues of ''Yoru no Funsui'', a condition that effectively compelled the project to cease. The Getty Museum similarly notes this closure as a result of authorities' concern, highlighting the lived realities of censorship that defined his practice rather than viewing his work as a purely stylistic affiliation.
The tightening of state control also reshaped avant-garde artistic organization. Yamamoto was involved with Nagoya-based collectives and initiatives in the late 1930s and early 1940s that dissolved or reorganized under wartime pressure, a context that informed the political edge of his Surrealist practice.
During the early 1940s, as censorship tightened and paper shortages intensified, Yamamoto continued to build “small infrastructures” for avant-garde exchange. Working with the Nagoya-based photography group Seidōsha, he edited the newsletter CARNET BLEU (confirmed issues 1941–1942), mixing photographs, polemical notes, and translated texts in a format that kept experimental discourse circulating under conditions hostile to avant-garde visibility. In essays from this period he repeatedly returned to the problem of constraint and agency, insisting that the task of form was not decorative novelty but the discovery of latitude “even within” imposed limits—a premise that resonates with later readings of his imagery of cages, silence, and enclosure.
A Nagoya City Art Museum collection catalogue interprets Yamamoto’s still-life photograph of a telephone receiver placed outside a birdcage as a Surrealist metaphor for the “absence of voice,” framing it as a form of silent resistance to wartime suppression of speech and writing.

Nagoya-based avant-garde circulation and national visibility
For Yamamoto, Nagoya’s avant-garde visibility was not a merely local background but the concrete field in which his early Surrealist commitments became publicly legible through clubs, magazines, and small-group publishing.
Taka Ishii Gallery notes that with the launch of Dokuritsu (Independent) in 1931 and the formation of the Nagoya Photo Avant-Garde in 1939, Nagoya became a major center for avant-garde photography in Japan, second only to Tokyo and Osaka. Echoing this account of Nagoya’s prominence, the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s wall text for Surrealism Beyond Borders situates Surrealism in 1920s–1930s Japan within interlinked networks of photo clubs that held regular meetings, competitions, and exhibitions, describing Nagoya as among the movement’s liveliest centers. It further observes that, as preparations for the Pacific War mounted, groups changed names and masked Surrealist activity under state disapproval, and that by 1941 Surrealists, communists, and others deemed subversive were being arrested around the country. In this climate, Yamamoto’s club-and-magazine circuits functioned as the practical infrastructure through which a Nagoya-based Surrealist photography could be produced, theorized, and made nationally legible under censorship, while remaining distinct from state-aligned documentary and propagandistic uses of the medium.
Stojković notes that in 1920s–1930s Japan, photography was largely cultivated within amateur photo clubs and an expansive culture of photographic magazines; together these formed a shashinkai (a photography “world”) before photographs were institutionally collected or had a stable market. She argues that Surrealism moved through these club-and-print channels in multiple routes—via firsthand encounters abroad, imported publications, translations, and reproductions—and found especially fertile ground outside Tokyo in cities such as Osaka and Nagoya, in part because these settings could operate away from the most intense glare of state censorship.
As comparative context for Yamamoto’s Nagoya-based activity within this shashinkai infrastructure, Stojković points to Osaka as an example of the club routines and collaborative norms that made Surrealist-leaning work publicly legible. For Osaka, Stojković highlights the long-lived Naniwa Shashin Kurabu (founded 1904) and the progressive Tanpei Shashin Kurabu (founded 1930), where Surrealist-leaning experimentation was cultivated through collective practice. She describes how Yasui Nakaji developed an object-based method he termed han seibutsu (“semi-still life”) in 1932—finding and arranging objects into evocative compositions—and how Tanpei members intensified this approach through themed shooting excursions that made Surrealist procedures compatible with club life and collaborative production. These Osaka examples illustrate the practical, collective mechanics—theme-based shoots, shared methods, and serial discussion—through which Surrealist-leaning experimentation circulated publicly; Yamamoto’s Nagoya-based work likewise entered public view through clubs and print circulation.
Stojković further situates this Osaka–Nagoya surge in direct relation to the 1937 Kaigai Chōgenjitsushugi Sakuhin ten (Exhibition of Foreign Surrealist Works), organized by Shūzō Takiguchi and Chirū Yamanaka with assistance from European Surrealists including Paul Éluard, Georges Hugnet, and Roland Penrose. In response, photographers such as Hanawa Gingo and Hirai Terushichi formed the Avangyarudo Zōei Shūdan (Avant-Garde Image Group), developing collaborative work grounded in “displacement” strategies that circulated widely through exhibitions and photographic magazines at the movement’s 1937–38 peak. This Osaka–Nagoya ecology forms the immediate context for Yamamoto’s own Nagoya-based Surrealist practice and for the local-to-national visibility he achieved through magazines, debates, and small-group publishing in the late 1930s.
Munro similarly describes Surrealism in Nagoya as flourishing under Chirū Yamanaka’s influence and taking a distinctly photographic form; she notes that in 1935 Yamamoto formed a Nagoya-based photography group with Yamanaka, Yoshio Shimozato, and Minoru Sakata. She adds that Sakata and Shimozato later acted as ambassadors for Surrealism, visiting the Fukuoka-based Surrealist photographic group Société IRF (Irf; Japanese: ソシエテ・イルフ) in 1940—an exchange that led to the publication of the Society’s sole commemorative journal issue.
Stojković records that after touring Tokyo, Kyoto, and Osaka, the 1937 Kaigai Chōgenjitsushugi Sakuhin ten was presented at Nagoya’s Maruzen garō (Maruzen Gallery) in July 1937, stimulating reorganizations and new collectives with explicitly Surrealist agendas in the city. Stojković notes that the Nagoya Abangarudo Kurabu (Nagoya Avant-Garde Club), formed at the end of 1937 under the euphemistic label “avant-garde,” included leading figures such as Yamamoto, a poet and photographer who had already been working in a distinct Surrealist mode since the turn of the decade.
A later overview described the Nagoya Avant-Garde Club as a cross-disciplinary avant-garde research group spanning photography, literature, painting, sculpture, and design, from which the photo section later split off as the Nagoya Photo Avant-Garde.
In February 1939, Yamamoto participated in the establishment of Nagoya Photo Avant-Garde, alongside Tsugio Tajima, Minoru Sakata, Yoshio Shimozato, and Chirū Yamanaka, but withdrew later that year (November). An exhibition text published by MEM adds earlier context: in 1934 Minoru Sakata opened a camera and photography supply store in Nagoya that drew painter Yoshio Shimozato, poet Chirū Yamanaka, and photographers Tsugio Tajima and Taizō Inagaki; the circle coalesced as the avant-garde collective Nagoya Photo Gruppe. 
Takeba situates Yamamoto’s entry into Nagoya’s avant-garde circles—and the subsequent formation of Nagoya Photo Avant-Garde—within a sequence of debates staged in photography magazines that attempted to define “avant-garde photography” at a national scale. In September 1938, Photo Times convened an “avant-garde photography” roundtable that brought Kansai and Tokyo photographers into direct debate over the emerging term; Sakata—already active as a critic—attended and made a strong impression, and at the end of 1938 the Cameraman editorial office organized a further roundtable in Nagoya with painters and poet-critics, later published in February 1939 as a “reexamination” of avant-garde photography that probed differences between Surrealism and abstraction, Surrealist beauty, and photographic automatism through extensive international examples. Takeba characterizes this forum as the first occasion on which Kansai and Tokyo photographers met directly to survey and explain the emerging field, and he suggests that Sakata’s intervention there positioned him not only as a practitioner but as a polemicist able to name and organize the movement’s terms. Stojković likewise records a December 1938 discussion in Nagoya among Minoru Sakata, Yoshio Shimozato, and Chirū Yamanaka—transcribed in the February 1939 issue of the local magazine Kameraman—as a moment of self-definition in debates over zen’ei shashin (avant-garde photography). 
In Takeba’s account, the collective—now including Yamamoto as a poet member—became visible nationwide as a programmatic Nagoya-based group, but the attempt to sustain a productive coordination between “photo-surrealism” and “photo-abstraction” proved fragile as the late-1930s cultural field shifted under militarism and the ascent of news photography. Takeba records that the original Nagoya Photo Avant-Garde dissolved in November 1939, and he frames the break between Sakata and Yamamoto as an unresolved disagreement over whether photographic innovation could be reconciled with nationalism—a pressure that would only intensify as wartime cultural policy narrowed the space for avant-garde work. 
Stojković records Yamamoto’s later recollection that a dispute with Sakata Minoru—over a proposal to couple “nationalism” with “innovative photography”—prompted him to leave the Nagoya club milieu. 
MEM adds that Nagoya Photo Avant-Garde emerged when the photo division of the Nagoya Avant-Garde Club split off; it further notes that after the group’s dissolution Sakata shifted toward ethnographic photography influenced by the mingei (folk craft) movement, while Yamamoto remained committed to avant-garde practice. The MEM text also notes that magazines such as Photo Times and Cameraman carried broader discussions of avant-garde photography and surrealism, helping catalyze new photographic movements in the late 1930s.
Across accounts, Yamamoto emerges here less as a peripheral participant than as the figure who draws the clearest line between Surrealist experimentation and state-aligned photographic agendas as the late-1930s field narrows under militarism. According to Maddox, Yamamoto severed ties with the Nagoya Photo Avant-Garde in 1939 when, under pressure to avoid attracting the Tokkō(the Thought Police), the group shifted toward producing propagandistic images that endorsed a “union, through photography, of reform and nationalism.” Aoki cites a 1939 diary entry in which Yamamoto wrote that the Nagoya Photo Avant-Garde “took its last breath”. Munro similarly records that as local photography organizations adopted explicitly nationalist aims, Yamamoto resigned in protest, drawing a clear line between his practice and state-aligned photographic agendas in the late 1930s and early 1940s. Iizawa notes that political pressure was exerted on the group in part because the term “avant-garde” itself invited suspicion—suggesting sympathies with the Russian communist avant-garde of the 1920s—and that, to avoid the attention of the Tokkō, the association renamed itself the Nagoya Shashin Bunka Kyōkai (Nagoya Photography Culture Association) in 1939 and was later compelled to dissolve in 1941. Takeba notes that the tendency’s terminology also shifted from zen’ei to zōkei—a neologism apparently inspired by Moholy-Nagy’s term “photo-plastic” and chosen for its comparatively benign connotations. By the late 1930s, “avant-garde” (zen’ei) often functioned as a euphemistic label for surrealist and abstract orientations under intensifying surveillance; the Tokyo-based Zen’ei Shashin Kyōkai accordingly renamed itself the Shashin Zōkei Kenkyūkai (Photo Plasticity Research Association) in 1939.
Stojković notes that as conditions worsened, even Takiguchi—seeking European photographs for exhibition—remarked that, “owing to the particular conditions in our country,” submissions should be limited to works without “political provocation” or “erotic extremism,” underscoring the narrowing space in which Surrealist photography could circulate.
Stojković describes the photobook Mesemu zoku, Chōgenjitsushugi shashin-shū / Mesemb, 20 photographies surréalistes (1940), edited by Shimozato, as a major publication to emerge from Nagoya’s photo-avant-garde offshoots: produced collaboratively with specialist collectors of Mesembryanthemaceae (“mesemb”) plants, its photographs grant botanical subjects an anthropomorphic, erotically charged presence that underscores the role of eroticism within Surrealist thinking under intensifying wartime scrutiny.
As state surveillance tightened toward 1941, Stojković argues that the continuation of Surrealist activity increasingly depended on public camouflage, including the ambiguous label zōkei shashin (“plastic photography”), whose usage overlapped with state mobilizations of “traditional” aesthetic rhetoric even as artists sought to preserve experimental latitude.
Contemporary accounts note that this Nagoya-based Surrealist-inflected avant-garde visibility was amplified through photography magazines and exhibition circuits—via outlets such as Photo Times and Camera Art—giving the city’s experimental work a national profile well before postwar institutional reassessments. Takeba emphasizes that Sakata’s role in this circuit was not only organizational but theoretical: after moving to Nagoya in 1934 and opening a Kodak-affiliated shop that served as a hub for amateurs, he began publishing photo theory in 1937 and contributed dozens of articles to amateur magazines through early 1941. Among these, his four-part series “Photo-abstraction and Photo-surrealism” (Shashin Geppō, from December 1937) was the first to classify the emergent avant-garde in these terms with examples, and his subsequent essays in 1939 reproduced Alfred H. Barr Jr.’s chart from MoMA’s Cubism and Abstract Art, underscoring his effort to locate “avant-garde photography” within a modern-art genealogy rather than a purely photographic lineage; Takeba also characterizes Sakata’s own image-making as shaped by German Neue Sachlichkeit and close-up attention to objects, yet oriented toward abstraction rather than straightforward objectivity. As an example of this critical recognition, Kaneko highlights a review in the July 1940 issue of Photo Times by photographer Minoru Sakata, who praised Yamamoto’s ability to “sublimate … poetic sentiments in silver bromide,” characterizing him as a “poet of silver bromide.” A chronology in the Nagoya City Art Museum’s 1989 exhibition catalogue records that the July 1940 issue of Photo Times carried Minoru Sakata’s profile “People promoting photography: Kansuke Yamamoto” (Japanese: 写真を推進する人々 山本悍右氏; Shashin o suishin suru hitobito: Yamamoto Kansuke-shi) and reproduced three of Yamamoto’s works. Within this media ecology, Yamamoto is the central case through which the section’s larger claim becomes legible: Surrealist photography in Japan was made not only in images but in debates, serial publication, and strategic self-positioning under censorship, with Yamamoto’s refusal of nationalist alignment serving as a defining ethical and aesthetic boundary.

VOU and a long-running cross-media axis
He became a member of "VOU" in 1939, belonging until it was dissolved in 1978.  Yamamoto’s association with VOU and its exhibitions would provide a long-running axis for his cross-disciplinary practice across the prewar and postwar decades.
Kaneko, Toda, and Vartanian note that as VOU members began submitting photographs in the late 1950s, poet Katsue Kitasono started making photographs under the instruction of Kansuke Yamamoto, who had been part of VOU since the prewar period.
The avant-garde poetry group VOU, led by poet Katsue Kitasono, was active from 1935 to 1978 (with an interruption during the Pacific War) and typically comprised about twenty-five to thirty-five members at a time. According to translator John Solt, VOU’s members included musicians, architects, technologists, and visual artists, yet all wrote poetry, reflecting a prewar conviction that poetry was “the fountain of all the arts.” Yamamoto joined VOU in 1939 and published poems in the group’s magazine as well as in other venues.
In a 2024 monograph on VOU and its editor-poet Kitasono, Bory and Donguy describe Yamamoto as the group’s most experimental photographer, adding that he exhibited regularly while rarely publishing photographs in the journal itself. In VOU no. 53 (1956), Kitasono praised Yamamoto’s photographic series as “poetic”, as reported by Bory and Donguy.
Fleming-Brown describes a 1941 still-life composition published in VOU in which a disconnected telephone receiver is staged as an offering on a plate at the end of a staircase descending toward the sea, exemplifying Yamamoto’s practice of placing everyday objects into symbolically charged constellations. In her account, Yamamoto’s accompanying text stresses photography’s mechanical organisation and its capacity to disclose objects in unforeseen relations—aligning his method with Surrealism’s pursuit of ruptures in assumed relations between perception and meaning. Fleming-Brown further notes that the 1941 issue was prefaced by a coerced declaration of support for Japan’s war effort; read against that context, she interprets the telephone image as continuous with Yamamoto’s wartime motif of disrupted communication and as an oblique resistance to the silencing of critical thought under authoritarian repression.
Richardson notes that Yamamoto’s work was prominently published in Kitasono’s VOU and other Japanese photography magazines, resulting in an unusually extensive published Surrealist portfolio.

Surveillance, censorship, and the politics of Surrealist form
Maddox situates Yamamoto’s wartime and immediate prewar activity within conditions shaped by the Peace Preservation Law (1925) and the Tokkō (Special Higher Police), under which avant-garde circles could be monitored and practices of nonconformity treated as grounds for suspicion. Munro argues that wartime cultural policing in Japan targeted ideology and perceived political content rather than “Western style” as such, noting that Western-influenced idioms could also be mobilized for state propaganda—an ambiguity that complicates accounts of repression as purely stylistic exclusion. She argues that as Tokkō enforcement intensified in the 1930s, the threat of persecution became so extreme that many avant-garde writers and artists "began to strip their work of any liberal, potentially subversive content." In contrast to this climate of self-censorship, Maddox writes that Yamamoto "quietly challenged the idea that Surrealist work needed to be devoid of provocation, politics, or thought," sustaining a critical charge through oblique form rather than direct declaration. Framing Surrealism as a practice often pursued under conditions of social convention and authoritarian control, D'Alessandro and Gale note that under rising militarism in late-1930s Japan, Surrealists such as Yamamoto Kansuke (figs. 65, 66), Shūzō Takiguchi, and Ichirō Fukuzawa were suspected of communist sympathies and arrested by the Tokubetsu Keisatsu (Special Higher Police), colloquially known as the “thought police”.
Munro documents how state pressure operated not only through censorship but through the surveillance of avant-garde social space. She notes that plain-clothes police attended Surrealist meetings from 1940, and records an explicit case of a Surrealist photographer agreeing to report on meetings on behalf of the police. In this tightening climate, groups also recalibrated themselves toward patriotic aims: Munro observes that the Nagoya Photography Club adopted the stated goal of a “union, through photography, of reform and nationalism,” prompting Yamamoto to resign in protest; the group later dissolved in 1941.
Institutional accounts have framed Yamamoto’s Surrealism not only as a stylistic alignment with European avant-gardes but as a sustained critical posture formed under conditions of political constraint. In the Getty Museum’s presentation, Yamamoto is characterized as an “ardent nonconformist” who consistently favored avant-garde modes of expression as a way of engaging modern Japanese life obliquely rather than through documentary realism, a stance that aligns his prewar publishing activities with a longer trajectory of art as criticism and dissent. Munro cautions against treating state repression as a simple function of Surrealism’s “Western” style, noting that Western-influenced idioms were also mobilized in official wartime propaganda and that enforcers could distinguish style from ideology. She observes that scholarship has alternated between describing Japanese Surrealism as apolitical and as politically radical enough to warrant systematic suppression, arguing that the movement’s political character is best assessed through close, practitioner-specific analysis rather than a single overarching narrative. In a diary entry from 1941, Yamamoto described art as arising from a “disobedient spirit against ready-made things of society,” presenting Surrealist practice as a refusal of conformity rather than a purely formal program.
Munro reports that a 1940 manuscript by Yamamoto, “Surrealism and Photography,” explicitly engages Surrealism’s political stakes by quoting Breton’s Communicating Vessels and discussing the movement’s tense relation to Communism, framing Surrealist “compulsive beauty” against revolutionary claims while continuing to argue for photography’s critical potential. In 1940, in his essay “A Concise Vilification with Regard to Photography,” Yamamoto described the photographic act as a process in which, once the shutter is released, “all things within a chosen angle fly into a fixed mask,” and framed his practice as a search for objects and for new correlations between them that could “symbolize living content.” Munro further notes that during the police investigation surrounding Yoru no Funsui (closed in 1939), Yamamoto was pressed to explain how his Surreal photography contributed to Japan’s war effort, underscoring the suspicion attached to his practice under wartime surveillance.
The closure of Yoru no Funsui under Tokkō (Special Higher Police) scrutiny has accordingly been discussed as more than an episode in publishing history: it marks the point at which Surrealist procedure—montage, displacement, and emblematic objects—became a practical means of negotiating restrictions on speech and association. Later institutional and market-facing interpretations have repeatedly returned to Yamamoto’s use of charged, everyday objects and claustrophobic enclosures as a visual vocabulary through which social pressure, surveillance, and constraint could be registered without direct declaration.
Maddox identifies a recurring vocabulary of suppression in Yamamoto’s wartime-era imagery, including a barred window as an emblem of imprisonment under the Peace Preservation Law, fedora hats clipped with clothespins or punctured by straight pins as metaphors for constrained thought, and a telephone trapped inside a birdcage as an image of enforced silence.

Postwar work and networks (1945–1960)
Japanese photographic historiography notes that around 1950—still under Allied occupation—efforts emerged to revive the prewar current often described as “avant-garde photography”, rooted in amateur circles such as Osaka’s Avant-Garde Zōei Shūdan and Nagoya’s Nagoya Foto Avant-Garde and characterized by Surrealism-inflected Shinkō Shashin techniques.
A chronology compiled by Yamamoto Toshio records that Yamamoto married Hisae Hirai in 1942; she later served as a model for a number of his postwar photographs.
After the war, Yamamoto emerged as a key organizer of Nagoya’s experimental scene. He co-founded the photographers’ collective VIVI-sha in 1947 and exhibited in its early shows, while also participating in the Bijutsu Bunka Kyōkai (Art and Culture Association) as a photography-section member, presenting works that treated the photograph as a constructed object rather than a transparent document. Kaneko, Toda, and Vartanian describe the Bijutsu Bunka Kyōkai—founded in 1939 by Surrealism-oriented avant-garde artists, curtailed after the 1941 arrests of leading figures, and reactivated in 1946—functioned as a key postwar base for cross-media avant-garde revival, underscoring how photography could align with contemporary art networks beyond the camera press. From 1949 he also produced publicity photographs as a commissioned photographer for Aichi Prefecture, a dual position—public-image labor alongside private experimentation—that sharpened the satirical edge and material intelligence of his postwar work.

Organizing the postwar avant-garde: Nagoya as an alternative centre
After World War II, Yamamoto resumed his activity as a central organizer of the Nagoya avant-garde, positioning the city as a critical cultural counter-pole to the realism that began to dominate Tokyo’s photographic circles. Curatorial accounts of Nagoya’s modern photography describe the postwar period as one in which realist and subjective approaches “vied closely”, following the renewed presence of Surrealist expression in the region. He participated in and founding a succession of groups, most notably "VIVI" (formed in 1947), which he formed with Minayoshi Takada, Keiichirō Gotō, and Yoshifumi Hattori. A chronology compiled by Yamamoto Toshio records that Yamamoto exhibited works including Yūutsu na sanpo (憂鬱な散歩), Jiikufurīdo gensō (ジイクフリイド幻想), A Chronicle of Drifting (漂流記), and Icarus’s Episode (イカルス挿話) at the second VIVI exhibition at Maruzen Gallery in 1949. Two of the works shown—Icarus’s Episode (1949) and A Chronicle of Drifting (1949)—are held by the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) and the J. Paul Getty Museum, respectively. Maddox writes that Yamamoto founded this group in order to keep the spirit of Surrealist ideology alive in the postwar period. In his movement-history of Nagoya photography, Takeba remarks that postwar Surrealist work has often been comparatively overlooked in accounts that privilege prewar avant-garde production, and he situates Yamamoto’s postwar activity alongside the VIVI circle in direct tension with contemporaneous realist currents. Takeba further notes that VIVI disseminated its postwar program through its bulletin CARNET DE VIVI, whose first issue (printed June 1948) paired members’ photographs with short programmatic statements and framed the collective as a renewed avant-garde after the wartime rupture. In Takeba’s reading, Yamamoto’s contribution links photographic trust to an awareness of the medium’s risks, explicitly reconnecting postwar practice to the ethical problem he had already posed through wartime translation work. Takeba places this local contest within a broader postwar polarization between socially oriented documentary realism and a renewed, formally constructed “subjective” photography, framing Yamamoto’s Surrealist revival as a third position grounded in montage, emblematic objects, and oblique critique.

Public-sector commissions and a dual register of practice
Alongside his renewed activity in postwar artist-run and experimental circles in Nagoya, Yamamoto also undertook photographic work within the public sector. A chronology compiled by Yamamoto Toshio records that from April 1949 he produced publicity photographs as a contracted contributor for Aichi Prefecture’s public relations office, an institutional commission that ran in parallel with his independent Surrealist activity and group-based exhibition work.
A chronology compiled by Yamamoto Toshio records additional examples of Yamamoto’s media-facing work in 1950. These included reproduction of a photograph in Shashin Techō (vol. 2, no. 5) as part of the roundtable “Zen’ei shashin o kataru zadankai” (“Roundtable on avant-garde photography”) on 1 January 1950, and publication of his photograph Idō shinzō—kōfuku no kage (“Heart in Motion—Shadow of Happiness”—now in the collection of the Art Institute of Chicago) in the Shintōkai Shimbun on 25 January 1950, accompanied by a short thriller by mystery writer Motomasa Hattori. A portrait photograph of Isamu Noguchi by Yamamoto was published in the Shintōkai Shimbun on 15 July 1950. From 13–26 September 1950, he contributed a 13-part newspaper series titled Kōhī no hanashi (Coffee talk) to the Shintōkai Shimbun.

Travel and postwar subject matter
The same chronology also records that in 1954 Yamamoto visited Hiroshima and Nagasaki and made photographs titled Hiroshima (1954) and Nagasaki (1954), indicating that his postwar practice extended beyond commissioned work into travel-based independent production. The Getty Museum’s exhibition, Japan’s Modern Divide, featured two vintage prints by Kansuke Yamamoto depicting stone statues that survived the atomic bombing.

Artist-run groups and durable networks
